messages.subject: Legend does not appear in PCA plot when using plotTangentSpace function, even when legend=TRUE.
messages.subject_clean: Legend does not appear in PCA plot when using plotTangentSpace function, even when legend=TRUE.
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I just wanted to check if anybody face this problem: even when legend=TRUE is added, PCA plot using plotTangentSpace does not create a legend. When I try to add a legend separately using legend base function, it does not work on the PCA plot although code works perfectly fine on an empty plot.

Is this a problem with Geomorph package and can it be circumvented for now?

Regards
RD

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Legend does not appear in PCA plot when using plotTangentSpace function, even when legend=TRUE.
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Legend does not appear in PCA plot when using plotTangentSpace function, even when legend=TRUE.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Rochishnu,

There might be something inherent with your data that is causing this issue or an issue with the function that is sprung by your data, as the function produces a legend when I use it.  Your intuition to try to add a legend is a good one, and this is how it works with gm.prcomp, a multi-use PCA function that is now available, which allows plot parameters to be adjusted as the user likes.  In fact, plotTangentSpace will be deprecated with the next geomorph release in lieu of better plotting flexibility with gm.prcomp.

If you check out the examples with gm.prcomp, you might get some inspiration for how to add your own legends or vary plot parameters.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Legend does not appear in PCA plot whenusing plotTangentSpace function, even when legend=TRUE.
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Legend does not appear in PCA plot whenusing plotTangentSpace function, even when legend=TRUE.
messages.body_plain:
I did the same thing and it worked perfectly for me.  However, I subsequently made my plot window much smaller and tried again, and the legend disappeared by virtue of being cut off.  You might consider increasing the size of your plot window and trying again.  If that fails, I would recommend reinstalling geomorph and/or R.

This is a problem with plotTangentSpace and why it is being deprecated.  Optimal plotting in R allows layers to be added to existing plots.  Because plotTangentSpace has multiple plots in one (the deformation grids are plots too), everything has to be created a priori and then cannot be adjusted.  If the plot window is too small, the legend might not work right.

In addition to gm.prcomp, picknplot.shape allows one to generate deformation grids anywhere in the plot without altering the plot.  Here is the general set up:

PCA <- gm.prcomp(coords, …)
myPlot <- plot(PCA)
picknplot.shape(myPlot) # can make as many deformation grids as desired
legend(…) # add a legend
points(…) # add additional points
text(…) # add text in the plot
title(…) # add a title, if desired
# etc…

None of the above can be done with plotTangentSpace.

The help page for picknplot.shape has more examples with real data.

Best,
Mike

Dear Mike,

You were correct in pointing out the problem of plotTangentSpace when using a smaller display window that is default in R studio. I could get the legend in a larger output window.

Anyways, I have also tried using gm.prcomp as you suggested. It is more flexible and I got the desired result using it. However, in its summary it does not give me the standard deviation in the first row that princomp/prcomp provides. Also, data_pca$sdev, does not automatically give me the standard deviations. Is there a way to get the standard deviation with gm.prcomp?

Regards

Rochishnu

messages.body_plain:
Rochishnu,

One of the objects returned by gm.prcomp is a vector of singular values, $d, which is the same as eigenvalues.  In the summary.gm.prcomp, these are provided instead of standard deviations but if standard deviations are preferred, one can get the square-root of these values; i.e., sqrt(data_pca$d).

Cheers!
Mike

> On Jun 4, 2019, at 7:06 AM, Rochishnu Dutta <rochish...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Dear Mike,
>
> You were correct in pointing out the problem of plotTangentSpace when using a smaller display window that is default in R studio. I could get the legend in a larger output window.
>
> Anyways, I have also tried using gm.prcomp as you suggested. It is more flexible and I got the desired result using it. However, in its summary it does not give me the standard deviation in the first row that princomp/prcomp provides. Also, data_pca$sdev, does not automatically give me the standard deviations. Is there a way to get the standard deviation with gm.prcomp?
>
> Regards
> Rochishnu
> From: Mike Collyer
> Sent: 03 June 2019 17:10
> To: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com
> Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Legend does not appear in PCA plot whenusingplotTangentSpace function, even when legend=TRUE.
>
> I did the same thing and it worked perfectly for me.  However, I subsequently made my plot window much smaller and tried again, and the legend disappeared by virtue of being cut off.  You might consider increasing the size of your plot window and trying again.  If that fails, I would recommend reinstalling geomorph and/or R.
>
> This is a problem with plotTangentSpace and why it is being deprecated.  Optimal plotting in R allows layers to be added to existing plots.  Because plotTangentSpace has multiple plots in one (the deformation grids are plots too), everything has to be created a priori and then cannot be adjusted.  If the plot window is too small, the legend might not work right.
>
> In addition to gm.prcomp, picknplot.shape allows one to generate deformation grids anywhere in the plot without altering the plot.  Here is the general set up:
>
> PCA <- gm.prcomp(coords, …)
> myPlot <- plot(PCA)
> picknplot.shape(myPlot) # can make as many deformation grids as desired
> legend(…) # add a legend
> points(…) # add additional points
> text(…) # add text in the plot
> title(…) # add a title, if desired
> # etc…
>
> None of the above can be done with plotTangentSpace.
>
> The help page for picknplot.shape has more examples with real data.
>
> Best,
> Mike
>
>

In fact, plotTangentSpace will be deprecated with the next geomorph release in lieu of better plotting flexibility with gm.prcomp.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm try to explore RRPP package, i want to runn the examples with a mixed model using PupfishHeads data:

PupfishHeads$logHeadSize <- log(PupfishHeads$headSize)
fit <- lm.rrpp(logHeadSize ~ sex + locality/year,
SS.type = "I", data = PupfishHeads,
print.progress = FALSE)
summary(fit)

but despite the linear model run and  i got results, the next messsage appear:

Warning: Because variables in the linear model are redundant
the linear model design has been truncated (via QR decomposition).
Original X columns: 13
Final X columns (rank): 9
Check coefficients or degrees of freedom in ANOVA to see changes.

However  I am using package data, somebody know if that is a error from the package?

thank you!!

Ana

Ana Celia Montes de Oca-Aguilar

messages.body_plain:
Karen,

One should perform GPA on all specimens combined, not species by species. Then, one can obtain the species means, and put these into a new object for the phylomorphospace function.

Obtaining species means is conveniently done using ‘coords.subet’ and then a lapply loop with ‘mshape’.  The example in the help file of that function will show you how.

Best,

messages.body_plain:
Hi again all,

     I recently stumbled on an analysis plsDA (partial least squares-discriminant analysis) that could potentially be more appropriate for my study and I wondered what you all thought. I am trying to explore the patterns of covariation between the shape of my 92 fish species (shape of each individual measured has been averaged within species) and my suite of multi-leveled categorical environmental factors. So, this is obviously a very preliminary and exploratory study in nature. From the little I have read so far it seems like most people do not use or advise using plsDA, but there was a note that it may be an appropriate method for exploratory studies. What I really want to be able to show is the strength of relationship between my two blocks and transformation grids of what particular shape is associated with each combination of the levels of all my factors because I'm interested in the directionality of the relationship between shape and environment, not JUST whether there is one. Does that make sense?

   If this seems feasible I would love to hear what you all think and suggest and/or if you have any citations I can check out to make this all happen I'd really appreciate it. Thanks for all you do to help!

Jessica

messages.subject_clean: Isolating shape and size
messages.body_plain: Freckleton (2009) states that using residuals as data should be avoided in phylogenetic comparative analyses (see Table 1) because it results in biases, particularly when the predictors are collinear. I want to remove the effects of size from my shape dataset so I can make inferences of shape and size separately. Should I be going about this differently? Freckleton (2009) suggests using multipredictor analyses rather than univariate methods and says do not use residuals in model fitting.
messages.body_snippet: Freckleton (2009) states that using residuals as data should be avoided in phylogenetic comparative analyses (see Table 1) because it results in biases, particularly when the predictors are collinear.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Isolating shape and size
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Isolating shape and size
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

Note that Bob’s recommendations were evaluated for univariate response data; though in this case they apply to multivariate data as well.  One option is to account for shape allometry in a phylogenetic context using procD.pgls, rather than procD.lm.  Then, residuals from this analysis have accounted for size, while also taking phylogenetic non-independence into account.

Dean

Freckleton (2009) states that using residuals as data should be avoided in phylogenetic comparative analyses (see Table 1) because it results in biases, particularly when the predictors are collinear. I want to remove the effects of size from my shape dataset so I can make inferences of shape and size separately. Should I be going about this differently? Freckleton (2009) suggests using multipredictor analyses rather than univariate methods and says do not use residuals in model fitting.

Hi Dean,

I got the same result when I did it that way. Below is the code I used in geomorph and scatterplot of the correlation between the residuals from procD.lm and procD.pgls. Am I doing something incorrectly with the code here?

Thanks,
Nick

# obtain size-adjusted residuals (and allometry-free shapes)
beak_CS_anova <- procD.lm(two.d.array(shape)~log(size), data = gdf, iter = 999, RRPP=TRUE, print.progress = TRUE)
summary(beak_CS_anova) #same ANOVA Table
shape.resid <- arrayspecs(beak_CS_anova$residuals, p=dim(land)[1], k=dim(land)[2]) #get allometry-adjusted residuals
adj.shape <- shape.resid + array(mshape(land), dim(land)) #get allometry-free shapes

# obtain size-adjusted residuals (and allometry-free shapes while taking into account phylogeny)
beak_CS_phy_anova <- procD.pgls(two.d.array(shape)~log(size), data = gdf, tree, iter = 999, print.progress = TRUE)
summary(beak_CS_phy_anova)
shape.resid.phy <- arrayspecs(beak_CS_phy_anova$residuals, p=dim(land)[1], k=dim(land)[2]) #get allometry-adjusted residuals
adj.shape.phy <- shape.resid.phy + array(mshape(land), dim(shape.resid.phy)) #get allometry-free shapes

plot(beak_CS_anova$residuals ~ beak_CS_phy_anova$residuals)

messages.body_plain:
I found the issue. I was not seeing $pgls.residuals because I was using the formula two.d.array(shape)~log(size). When I used the formula shape~log(size) with procD.pgls, I was able to get $pgls.residuals. Both $residuals and $pgls.residuals were 99% correlated (plot attached). I did a pca on $residuals and $pgls.residuals, the first few axes were nearly perfectly correlated but this relationship started to break down in higher level PCs.

On Sunday, June 9, 2019 at 3:22:26 PM UTC-7, Nick wrote:

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Geomorph community,

I found this post very interesting as I want to visualize allometry corrected shapes on  PCA. I have no significant interaction between size and group (5 species), so I followed the step that Michael advised on the first thread. However I lost all species differences on my shape space.
My R-squared is 0.14 for the size variable, and 0.51 for my group variable. So I have quite distinct intercepts that explain half of the sample's variation, and I am wondering if that is why I loose discrimination in the morphospace when I use the residuals from procD.lm(shape~log(size)+species). I tried to use the RSC's from procD.allometry(shape~log(size),f2=~species) but obtained a similar result when I tried to visualize differences on a morphospace.

However, when I tried pairwise<-advanced.procD.lm(shape ~ log(size)+species, ~1,groups = ~species, angle.type = "deg", iter = 9999, data = gdf), I still obtained significant differences between species.

I therefore have two questions I'd like to ask you:
1) Should a PCA on allometry-corrected shapes not reflect what I got from the means comparison?
2) In my case, despite the common allometries between the five species, is the large r-squared for the group variable impeditive to the obtentian of allometry-corrected shapes acounting for group structure? Should I instead try to visualize differences with the residuals of procD.lm(shape~log(size))?

Thank you for your attention and for the present thread.

Best,
Carlos.

Le samedi 7 juillet 2018 00:42:48 UTC+2, Nicole Torres Tamayo a écrit :

> Dear Dean, Mike (and all),
>
> Thank you both for such extensive and clarifying explanations. My question is part of a revision process of a manuscript of mine, so your reply is very helpful for me. I will re-do the analyses according to your suggestions that definitely make sense.
>
> All the best,
>
> Nicole

> 2018-07-03 16:31 GMT+02:00 Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu>:

> > Nicole,
> >
> >
> >
> > The procedure of ‘removing’ the effect of some factor and treating residuals in downstream analyses, while simple to understand, is not something I generally advocate. Often times, this sort of procedure does not do what people think it is doing, and it can get one into trouble. I’ll return to your particular analysis below, but a quick example displaying the problems of using a residual approach rather than a factorial model will show why it should not be applied indiscriminately as a means of accounting for sources of variation.
> >
> >
> >
> > Say one has two species and wishes to know whether their head shapes differ.  However, one also knows there is allometry, so size-effects could complicate matters. Following the residual approach, it seems logical to perform a regression of shape on size (perhaps within each species) obtain the size-free shape residuals, and then perform an anova to compare the two species for their shape differences.  All is fine with this, yes?  NO. The residual-based approach can only arrive at an appropriate biological inference if and only if the patterns of allometry in each species are the same. If the allometric regressions differ across species, then the residuals from the regressions represent different things, and are no longer comparable; meaning the inference of the anova of residuals might not accurately describe the patterns in the data.
> >
> >
> >
> > To put it another way, what one really has here is an analysis of covariance model, where shape ~ size + group + size:group.   Using residuals from size regressions explicitly assumes that the size:group interaction is not significant, and the variation explained by the interaction is sufficiently small that the multivariate slopes may be treated as homogeneous.  Now if that is in fact the case, then the appropriate course of action is to fit the common slope model (shape ~ size+group) and compare groups while accounting for size. Under this very restricted case,  the residual approach might hope to arrive at a similar answer as compared to the common slope model.  But using the common slope model is simply more efficient and clear as to what one is investigating.
> >
> >
> >
> > However, if the allometry patterns differ between species, then the interaction term of the ancova would be significant. This, in turn, means that the slopoes are not directly comparable. It also means that one’s question has changed from: “Are my species different in shape” to: “How do allometry patterns differ between species?”.  The data have, in effect, changed your question.  Using residuals, one would not only be blind to this data reality (because it could not be asked), but also, it shows why the residual approach is wrong here. In this scenario, the residuals are representing different things in each species because the size-shape relationship is not concordant between species. Thus, using residuals one might incorrectly make inferences on general shape differences between species. Only by including various factors in the model, and their interaction, can one arrive at the correct inference.
> >
> >
> >
> > Now back  to your system. From what you have described you have a significant interaction, which, as you stated, implies that some aspect of sexual dimorphism differs between groups. That result demands further exploration and examination. How does sexual dimorphism differ? Is one species sexually dimorphic and the other not? Is the degree of sexual dimorphism greater in one population versus the other? Is the direction of sexual dimorphism similar of different in shape space? These are the questions to investigate now.  Note that trajectory analysis would be a particularly useful set of tools to utilize here; and in fact, have been used to examine and compare patterns of sexual dimorphism across groups (see Collyer and Adams, 2007; 2013: Adams and Collyer, 2007; 2009, etc.).
> >
> >
> >
> > To answer your last question about obtaining residuals separately for each population and using these; no.  That would be tantamount to the residuals from regression example above. Since the pop:sex interaction term is significant, residuals from a sex-model within populations are simply not comparable across them. Subsequent analyses into the nature of the sexual dimorphism are likely to be more fruitful in terms of extracting useful biological information.
> >
> >
> >
> > Hope this helps,
> >
> >
> >
> > Dean

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Carlos, and everyone,

I encourage everyone to think about what a null model is and why it is used as a basis for making inferences from a “full” model.  Carlos, your advanced.procD.lm scenario below does not make any sense because you use a null model that models species differences, a full model that adds size to the null model, and then ask if species are different?  Second, in the attempt to make “allometry-corrected” shapes, the residuals can come from only one model - an allometry model.  ~ size + species IS NOT an allometry model.

If one wants to ask if there are species differences, after accounting for allometry, FIRST COUNT FOR ALLOMETRY as a null model; i.e., shape ~ size.  After explaining that variation, are there species differences in the residual variation?  Full model = shape ~ size + species.

So how to visualize this?  Use residuals from the null model (and I would add the mean shape to these) and color code them by species, to see if there is a pattern in the scatter that suggest species are different.  If there is, then you know why adding species to your full model was a good idea  If not, then you know why adding it did not help.

I encourage every one to think of hypothesis testing as a model building exercise.  If I add effects to my model, does it help to explain my shape variation?  If I take effects away, do I loose my precision to estimate shapes?  Every hypothesis test is a model comparison - one with a set of effects (null or reduced) and the other with a set of effects plus one additional effect (full).  Every visualization tool should also be consistent with the process.

Carlos, if you get residuals from a model that has species and size as explanatory variable, OF COURSE there will be no evidence fo a species effect in a PCA of the residuals.  You have accounted for it in your model.  So your last comment was most astute.  Define your null model (shape ~ size), do a PCA on the residuals, check if there is a pattern the null model missed - that will show you how the effect, species, manifests in your data after accounting for allometry.

Mike

> On Jun 10, 2019, at 9:28 AM, Carlos Blanco <pien...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Dear Geomorph community,
>
> I found this post very interesting as I want to visualize allometry corrected shapes on  PCA. I have no significant interaction between size and group (5 species), so I followed the step that Michael advised on the first thread. However I lost all species differences on my shape space.
> My R-squared is 0.14 for the size variable, and 0.51 for my group variable. So I have quite distinct intercepts that explain half of the sample's variation, and I am wondering if that is why I loose discrimination in the morphospace when I use the residuals from procD.lm(shape~log(size)+species). I tried to use the RSC's from procD.allometry(shape~log(size),f2=~species) but obtained a similar result when I tried to visualize differences on a morphospace.
>
> However, when I tried pairwise<-advanced.procD.lm(shape ~ log(size)+species, ~1,groups = ~species, angle.type = "deg", iter = 9999, data = gdf), I still obtained significant differences between species.
>
> I therefore have two questions I'd like to ask you:
> 1) Should a PCA on allometry-corrected shapes not reflect what I got from the means comparison?
> 2) In my case, despite the common allometries between the five species, is the large r-squared for the group variable impeditive to the obtentian of allometry-corrected shapes acounting for group structure? Should I instead try to visualize differences with the residuals of procD.lm(shape~log(size))?
>
>
> Thank you for your attention and for the present thread.
>
> Best,
> Carlos.

> > Dear Dean, Mike (and all),
> >
> > Thank you both for such extensive and clarifying explanations. My question is part of a revision process of a manuscript of mine, so your reply is very helpful for me. I will re-do the analyses according to your suggestions that definitely make sense.
> >
> > All the best,
> >
> > Nicole
> >
> > 2018-07-03 16:31 GMT+02:00 Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu>:
> > >
> > > Nicole,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > The procedure of ‘removing’ the effect of some factor and treating residuals in downstream analyses, while simple to understand, is not something I generally advocate. Often times, this sort of procedure does not do what people think it is doing, and it can get one into trouble. I’ll return to your particular analysis below, but a quick example displaying the problems of using a residual approach rather than a factorial model will show why it should not be applied indiscriminately as a means of accounting for sources of variation.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Say one has two species and wishes to know whether their head shapes differ.  However, one also knows there is allometry, so size-effects could complicate matters. Following the residual approach, it seems logical to perform a regression of shape on size (perhaps within each species) obtain the size-free shape residuals, and then perform an anova to compare the two species for their shape differences.  All is fine with this, yes?  NO. The residual-based approach can only arrive at an appropriate biological inference if and only if the patterns of allometry in each species are the same. If the allometric regressions differ across species, then the residuals from the regressions represent different things, and are no longer comparable; meaning the inference of the anova of residuals might not accurately describe the patterns in the data.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > To put it another way, what one really has here is an analysis of covariance model, where shape ~ size + group + size:group.   Using residuals from size regressions explicitly assumes that the size:group interaction is not significant, and the variation explained by the interaction is sufficiently small that the multivariate slopes may be treated as homogeneous.  Now if that is in fact the case, then the appropriate course of action is to fit the common slope model (shape ~ size+group) and compare groups while accounting for size. Under this very restricted case,  the residual approach might hope to arrive at a similar answer as compared to the common slope model.  But using the common slope model is simply more efficient and clear as to what one is investigating.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > However, if the allometry patterns differ between species, then the interaction term of the ancova would be significant. This, in turn, means that the slopoes are not directly comparable. It also means that one’s question has changed from: “Are my species different in shape” to: “How do allometry patterns differ between species?”.  The data have, in effect, changed your question.  Using residuals, one would not only be blind to this data reality (because it could not be asked), but also, it shows why the residual approach is wrong here. In this scenario, the residuals are representing different things in each species because the size-shape relationship is not concordant between species. Thus, using residuals one might incorrectly make inferences on general shape differences between species. Only by including various factors in the model, and their interaction, can one arrive at the correct inference.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Now back  to your system. From what you have described you have a significant interaction, which, as you stated, implies that some aspect of sexual dimorphism differs between groups. That result demands further exploration and examination. How does sexual dimorphism differ? Is one species sexually dimorphic and the other not? Is the degree of sexual dimorphism greater in one population versus the other? Is the direction of sexual dimorphism similar of different in shape space? These are the questions to investigate now.  Note that trajectory analysis would be a particularly useful set of tools to utilize here; and in fact, have been used to examine and compare patterns of sexual dimorphism across groups (see Collyer and Adams, 2007; 2013: Adams and Collyer, 2007; 2009, etc.).
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > To answer your last question about obtaining residuals separately for each population and using these; no.  That would be tantamount to the residuals from regression example above. Since the pop:sex interaction term is significant, residuals from a sex-model within populations are simply not comparable across them. Subsequent analyses into the nature of the sexual dimorphism are likely to be more fruitful in terms of extracting useful biological information.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Hope this helps,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Dean

Dear Geomorph Group Leads,

I am trying to run PCA with asymmetric component derived from bilat.symmetry implementation of matching symmetry analysis for the very first time.

My .TPS file do not have any missing values. However, when I looked into the asymmetric coordinates for each individual after bilat.symmetry analysis, I found that two individuals returned with NAs for all 11 landmarks I used. My first intuition is that there two individuals are absolutely symmetric such that they do not have any asymmetry. Am I correct in presuming it?

Secondly, since I would like to run PCA (with, say, plotTangentSpace) on the  asymmetric shape coordinates of individuals, is there a straight forward way to omit individuals with NA values? I could not find any solution on the net.

Regards
Rochishnu

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mike,

Than you very much for you answer and for your advices. I got confused about allometry-models, since I wanted to account for the fact that different species have different intercepts, and eventually use group predictions to obtain residuals from a common slope for all groups.

Thank you once again.

ps: Also, I just wanted to warn you that I believe to have found a bug in the new function plotAllometry. The values of residual shape component outputed by this function are actually normal principal component scores.

An example with the plethodon data set:

data(plethodon)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land, print.progress = FALSE)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, site = plethodon$site,species = plethodon$species)
fit2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ Csize * species, data=gdf, iter=4999, print.progress = FALSE)
plethodon_eg<-plotAllometry(fit2, size = gdf$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "CAC", pch = 19,col=gdf$species)
plot(plethodon_eg$RSC[,1],plethodon_eg$RSC[,2],pch=19,col=gdf$species)
PCA <- plotTangentSpace(gdf$coords, axis1 = 1, axis2 = 2, groups = gdf$species, legend = FALSE)

Le lundi 10 juin 2019 16:39:12 UTC+2, Michael Collyer a écrit :

> Dear Carlos, and everyone,
>
> I encourage everyone to think about what a null model is and why it is used as a basis for making inferences from a “full” model.  Carlos, your advanced.procD.lm scenario below does not make any sense because you use a null model that models species differences, a full model that adds size to the null model, and then ask if species are different?  Second, in the attempt to make “allometry-corrected” shapes, the residuals can come from only one model - an allometry model.  ~ size + species IS NOT an allometry model.
>
> If one wants to ask if there are species differences, after accounting for allometry, FIRST COUNT FOR ALLOMETRY as a null model; i.e., shape ~ size.  After explaining that variation, are there species differences in the residual variation?  Full model = shape ~ size + species.
>
> So how to visualize this?  Use residuals from the null model (and I would add the mean shape to these) and color code them by species, to see if there is a pattern in the scatter that suggest species are different.  If there is, then you know why adding species to your full model was a good idea  If not, then you know why adding it did not help.
>
> I encourage every one to think of hypothesis testing as a model building exercise.  If I add effects to my model, does it help to explain my shape variation?  If I take effects away, do I loose my precision to estimate shapes?  Every hypothesis test is a model comparison - one with a set of effects (null or reduced) and the other with a set of effects plus one additional effect (full).  Every visualization tool should also be consistent with the process.
>
> Carlos, if you get residuals from a model that has species and size as explanatory variable, OF COURSE there will be no evidence fo a species effect in a PCA of the residuals.  You have accounted for it in your model.  So your last comment was most astute.  Define your null model (shape ~ size), do a PCA on the residuals, check if there is a pattern the null model missed - that will show you how the effect, species, manifests in your data after accounting for allometry.
>
> Mike
>

> > On Jun 10, 2019, at 9:28 AM, Carlos Blanco <pien...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >

> > Dear Geomorph community,
> >
> > I found this post very interesting as I want to visualize allometry corrected shapes on  PCA. I have no significant interaction between size and group (5 species), so I followed the step that Michael advised on the first thread. However I lost all species differences on my shape space.
> > My R-squared is 0.14 for the size variable, and 0.51 for my group variable. So I have quite distinct intercepts that explain half of the sample's variation, and I am wondering if that is why I loose discrimination in the morphospace when I use the residuals from procD.lm(shape~log(size)+species). I tried to use the RSC's from procD.allometry(shape~log(size),f2=~species) but obtained a similar result when I tried to visualize differences on a morphospace.
> >
> > However, when I tried pairwise<-advanced.procD.lm(shape ~ log(size)+species, ~1,groups = ~species, angle.type = "deg", iter = 9999, data = gdf), I still obtained significant differences between species.
> >
> > I therefore have two questions I'd like to ask you:
> > 1) Should a PCA on allometry-corrected shapes not reflect what I got from the means comparison?
> > 2) In my case, despite the common allometries between the five species, is the large r-squared for the group variable impeditive to the obtentian of allometry-corrected shapes acounting for group structure? Should I instead try to visualize differences with the residuals of procD.lm(shape~log(size))?

> > > Dear Dean, Mike (and all),
> > >
> > > Thank you both for such extensive and clarifying explanations. My question is part of a revision process of a manuscript of mine, so your reply is very helpful for me. I will re-do the analyses according to your suggestions that definitely make sense.
> > >
> > > All the best,

> > > Nicole

> > > 2018-07-03 16:31 GMT+02:00 Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu>:
> > > >
> > > > Nicole,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > The procedure of ‘removing’ the effect of some factor and treating residuals in downstream analyses, while simple to understand, is not something I generally advocate. Often times, this sort of procedure does not do what people think it is doing, and it can get one into trouble. I’ll return to your particular analysis below, but a quick example displaying the problems of using a residual approach rather than a factorial model will show why it should not be applied indiscriminately as a means of accounting for sources of variation.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Say one has two species and wishes to know whether their head shapes differ.  However, one also knows there is allometry, so size-effects could complicate matters. Following the residual approach, it seems logical to perform a regression of shape on size (perhaps within each species) obtain the size-free shape residuals, and then perform an anova to compare the two species for their shape differences.  All is fine with this, yes?  NO. The residual-based approach can only arrive at an appropriate biological inference if and only if the patterns of allometry in each species are the same. If the allometric regressions differ across species, then the residuals from the regressions represent different things, and are no longer comparable; meaning the inference of the anova of residuals might not accurately describe the patterns in the data.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > To put it another way, what one really has here is an analysis of covariance model, where shape ~ size + group + size:group.   Using residuals from size regressions explicitly assumes that the size:group interaction is not significant, and the variation explained by the interaction is sufficiently small that the multivariate slopes may be treated as homogeneous.  Now if that is in fact the case, then the appropriate course of action is to fit the common slope model (shape ~ size+group) and compare groups while accounting for size. Under this very restricted case,  the residual approach might hope to arrive at a similar answer as compared to the common slope model.  But using the common slope model is simply more efficient and clear as to what one is investigating.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > However, if the allometry patterns differ between species, then the interaction term of the ancova would be significant. This, in turn, means that the slopoes are not directly comparable. It also means that one’s question has changed from: “Are my species different in shape” to: “How do allometry patterns differ between species?”.  The data have, in effect, changed your question.  Using residuals, one would not only be blind to this data reality (because it could not be asked), but also, it shows why the residual approach is wrong here. In this scenario, the residuals are representing different things in each species because the size-shape relationship is not concordant between species. Thus, using residuals one might incorrectly make inferences on general shape differences between species. Only by including various factors in the model, and their interaction, can one arrive at the correct inference.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Now back  to your system. From what you have described you have a significant interaction, which, as you stated, implies that some aspect of sexual dimorphism differs between groups. That result demands further exploration and examination. How does sexual dimorphism differ? Is one species sexually dimorphic and the other not? Is the degree of sexual dimorphism greater in one population versus the other? Is the direction of sexual dimorphism similar of different in shape space? These are the questions to investigate now.  Note that trajectory analysis would be a particularly useful set of tools to utilize here; and in fact, have been used to examine and compare patterns of sexual dimorphism across groups (see Collyer and Adams, 2007; 2013: Adams and Collyer, 2007; 2009, etc.).
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > To answer your last question about obtaining residuals separately for each population and using these; no.  That would be tantamount to the residuals from regression example above. Since the pop:sex interaction term is significant, residuals from a sex-model within populations are simply not comparable across them. Subsequent analyses into the nature of the sexual dimorphism are likely to be more fruitful in terms of extracting useful biological information.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Hope this helps,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Dean
> > > >

> > > > > I believe the advice you were given is that you should explicitly test whether there is a sex * population interaction.  If there is, you should not try to “correct” your shape data, as sexual dimorphism manifests differently in the different populations.  You can do that with
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > procD.lm(shape ~ sex * population)
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > If the  sex * population effect in the ANOVA is significant, do not correct shapes.  If not, you can use the residuals from a new model
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population)
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > which if added to the overall mean shape, will produce shapes that have held constant the effects of population and sex.  This is how I accomplish this:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > newshape <- procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population, iter = 1)$residuals + procD.lm(shape ~ 1, iter = 1)$fitted
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Keep in mind that you would also have to use arrayspecs to convert newshape back into an array rather than a matrix.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Again, the correction should be done IF, AND ONLY IF, you have determined there is not a meaningful interaction between sex and population.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers!
> > > > >
> > > > > Mike
> > > > >
> > > > >

> > > > >
> > > > > Nicole,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > The procedure of ‘removing’ the effect of some factor and treating residuals in downstream analyses, while simple to understand, is not something I generally advocate. Often times, this sort of procedure does not do what people think it is doing, and it can get one into trouble. I’ll return to your particular analysis below, but a quick example displaying the problems of using a residual approach rather than a factorial model will show why it should not be applied indiscriminately as a means of accounting for sources of variation.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Say one has two species and wishes to know whether their head shapes differ.  However, one also knows there is allometry, so size-effects could complicate matters. Following the residual approach, it seems logical to perform a regression of shape on size (perhaps within each species) obtain the size-free shape residuals, and then perform an anova to compare the two species for their shape differences.  All is fine with this, yes?  NO. The residual-based approach can only arrive at an appropriate biological inference if and only if the patterns of allometry in each species are the same. If the allometric regressions differ across species, then the residuals from the regressions represent different things, and are no longer comparable; meaning the inference of the anova of residuals might not accurately describe the patterns in the data.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > To put it another way, what one really has here is an analysis of covariance model, where shape ~ size + group + size:group.   Using residuals from size regressions explicitly assumes that the size:group interaction is not significant, and the variation explained by the interaction is sufficiently small that the multivariate slopes may be treated as homogeneous.  Now if that is in fact the case, then the appropriate course of action is to fit the common slope model (shape ~ size+group) and compare groups while accounting for size. Under this very restricted case,  the residual approach might hope to arrive at a similar answer as compared to the common slope model.  But using the common slope model is simply more efficient and clear as to what one is investigating.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > However, if the allometry patterns differ between species, then the interaction term of the ancova would be significant. This, in turn, means that the slopoes are not directly comparable. It also means that one’s question has changed from: “Are my species different in shape” to: “How do allometry patterns differ between species?”.  The data have, in effect, changed your question.  Using residuals, one would not only be blind to this data reality (because it could not be asked), but also, it shows why the residual approach is wrong here. In this scenario, the residuals are representing different things in each species because the size-shape relationship is not concordant between species. Thus, using residuals one might incorrectly make inferences on general shape differences between species. Only by including various factors in the model, and their interaction, can one arrive at the correct inference.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Now back  to your system. From what you have described you have a significant interaction, which, as you stated, implies that some aspect of sexual dimorphism differs between groups. That result demands further exploration and examination. How does sexual dimorphism differ? Is one species sexually dimorphic and the other not? Is the degree of sexual dimorphism greater in one population versus the other? Is the direction of sexual dimorphism similar of different in shape space? These are the questions to investigate now.  Note that trajectory analysis would be a particularly useful set of tools to utilize here; and in fact, have been used to examine and compare patterns of sexual dimorphism across groups (see Collyer and Adams, 2007; 2013: Adams and Collyer, 2007; 2009, etc.).
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > To answer your last question about obtaining residuals separately for each population and using these; no.  That would be tantamount to the residuals from regression example above. Since the pop:sex interaction term is significant, residuals from a sex-model within populations are simply not comparable across them. Subsequent analyses into the nature of the sexual dimorphism are likely to be more fruitful in terms of extracting useful biological information.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Hope this helps,

> > > > > > I believe the advice you were given is that you should explicitly test whether there is a sex * population interaction.  If there is, you should not try to “correct” your shape data, as sexual dimorphism manifests differently in the different populations.  You can do that with
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > procD.lm(shape ~ sex * population)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If the  sex * population effect in the ANOVA is significant, do not correct shapes.  If not, you can use the residuals from a new model
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > which if added to the overall mean shape, will produce shapes that have held constant the effects of population and sex.  This is how I accomplish this:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > newshape <- procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population, iter = 1)$residuals + procD.lm(shape ~ 1, iter = 1)$fitted
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Keep in mind that you would also have to use arrayspecs to convert newshape back into an array rather than a matrix.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Again, the correction should be done IF, AND ONLY IF, you have determined there is not a meaningful interaction between sex and population.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Cheers!

> > > Dear Carlos, and everyone,
> > >
> > > I encourage everyone to think about what a null model is and why it is used as a basis for making inferences from a “full” model.  Carlos, your advanced.procD.lm scenario below does not make any sense because you use a null model that models species differences, a full model that adds size to the null model, and then ask if species are different?  Second, in the attempt to make “allometry-corrected” shapes, the residuals can come from only one model - an allometry model.  ~ size + species IS NOT an allometry model.
> > >
> > > If one wants to ask if there are species differences, after accounting for allometry, FIRST COUNT FOR ALLOMETRY as a null model; i.e., shape ~ size.  After explaining that variation, are there species differences in the residual variation?  Full model = shape ~ size + species.
> > >
> > > So how to visualize this?  Use residuals from the null model (and I would add the mean shape to these) and color code them by species, to see if there is a pattern in the scatter that suggest species are different.  If there is, then you know why adding species to your full model was a good idea  If not, then you know why adding it did not help.
> > >
> > > I encourage every one to think of hypothesis testing as a model building exercise.  If I add effects to my model, does it help to explain my shape variation?  If I take effects away, do I loose my precision to estimate shapes?  Every hypothesis test is a model comparison - one with a set of effects (null or reduced) and the other with a set of effects plus one additional effect (full).  Every visualization tool should also be consistent with the process.
> > >
> > > Carlos, if you get residuals from a model that has species and size as explanatory variable, OF COURSE there will be no evidence fo a species effect in a PCA of the residuals.  You have accounted for it in your model.  So your last comment was most astute.  Define your null model (shape ~ size), do a PCA on the residuals, check if there is a pattern the null model missed - that will show you how the effect, species, manifests in your data after accounting for allometry.

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.body_plain:
Carlos,

Thanks for the clarification.  The RSC are (normalized) principal component scores, rotated according to the partial least squares association between the shape data and the size vector.  One might expect that the two plots look the same, except for a rotation.  However, because the size vector is a vector, and not a matrix, alignment of a matrix to a line produces the same current alignment of the matrix, meaning that RSC is a fancy name for PCA.

In fact, while I have the ear of the geomorph community, please let me express this emphatically.  CAC and RSC are no different than two-block PLS and PCA, respectively!  If one were to perform 2B-PLS instead of CAC, the first plot would be the same, i.e.,

> PLS = two.b.pls(log(Y.gpa$Csize), Y.gpa$coords)
> plot(PLS)
> fit <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize), data = gdf)
> PA <- plotAllometry(fit, Y.gpa$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "CAC”)

If we take this a step further and perform PCA, we can generate the second plot, easily

> PC <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)$x
> plot(PA$CAC[,1], PC[,1])

So not a bug.  It’s just that CAC and RSC are not really anything that special - just a redefinition of common terms for the purpose of allometry.

Mike

> > > Le lundi 10 juin 2019 16:39:12 UTC+2, Michael Collyer a écrit :
> > > > Dear Carlos, and everyone,
> > > >
> > > > I encourage everyone to think about what a null model is and why it is used as a basis for making inferences from a “full” model.  Carlos, your advanced.procD.lm scenario below does not make any sense because you use a null model that models species differences, a full model that adds size to the null model, and then ask if species are different?  Second, in the attempt to make “allometry-corrected” shapes, the residuals can come from only one model - an allometry model.  ~ size + species IS NOT an allometry model.
> > > >
> > > > If one wants to ask if there are species differences, after accounting for allometry, FIRST COUNT FOR ALLOMETRY as a null model; i.e., shape ~ size.  After explaining that variation, are there species differences in the residual variation?  Full model = shape ~ size + species.
> > > >
> > > > So how to visualize this?  Use residuals from the null model (and I would add the mean shape to these) and color code them by species, to see if there is a pattern in the scatter that suggest species are different.  If there is, then you know why adding species to your full model was a good idea  If not, then you know why adding it did not help.
> > > >
> > > > I encourage every one to think of hypothesis testing as a model building exercise.  If I add effects to my model, does it help to explain my shape variation?  If I take effects away, do I loose my precision to estimate shapes?  Every hypothesis test is a model comparison - one with a set of effects (null or reduced) and the other with a set of effects plus one additional effect (full).  Every visualization tool should also be consistent with the process.
> > > >
> > > > Carlos, if you get residuals from a model that has species and size as explanatory variable, OF COURSE there will be no evidence fo a species effect in a PCA of the residuals.  You have accounted for it in your model.  So your last comment was most astute.  Define your null model (shape ~ size), do a PCA on the residuals, check if there is a pattern the null model missed - that will show you how the effect, species, manifests in your data after accounting for allometry.

> > > > > > 2018-07-03 16:31 GMT+02:00 Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu <http://iastate.edu/>>:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Nicole,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > The procedure of ‘removing’ the effect of some factor and treating residuals in downstream analyses, while simple to understand, is not something I generally advocate. Often times, this sort of procedure does not do what people think it is doing, and it can get one into trouble. I’ll return to your particular analysis below, but a quick example displaying the problems of using a residual approach rather than a factorial model will show why it should not be applied indiscriminately as a means of accounting for sources of variation.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Say one has two species and wishes to know whether their head shapes differ.  However, one also knows there is allometry, so size-effects could complicate matters. Following the residual approach, it seems logical to perform a regression of shape on size (perhaps within each species) obtain the size-free shape residuals, and then perform an anova to compare the two species for their shape differences.  All is fine with this, yes?  NO. The residual-based approach can only arrive at an appropriate biological inference if and only if the patterns of allometry in each species are the same. If the allometric regressions differ across species, then the residuals from the regressions represent different things, and are no longer comparable; meaning the inference of the anova of residuals might not accurately describe the patterns in the data.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > To put it another way, what one really has here is an analysis of covariance model, where shape ~ size + group + size:group.   Using residuals from size regressions explicitly assumes that the size:group interaction is not significant, and the variation explained by the interaction is sufficiently small that the multivariate slopes may be treated as homogeneous.  Now if that is in fact the case, then the appropriate course of action is to fit the common slope model (shape ~ size+group) and compare groups while accounting for size. Under this very restricted case,  the residual approach might hope to arrive at a similar answer as compared to the common slope model.  But using the common slope model is simply more efficient and clear as to what one is investigating.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > However, if the allometry patterns differ between species, then the interaction term of the ancova would be significant. This, in turn, means that the slopoes are not directly comparable. It also means that one’s question has changed from: “Are my species different in shape” to: “How do allometry patterns differ between species?”.  The data have, in effect, changed your question.  Using residuals, one would not only be blind to this data reality (because it could not be asked), but also, it shows why the residual approach is wrong here. In this scenario, the residuals are representing different things in each species because the size-shape relationship is not concordant between species. Thus, using residuals one might incorrectly make inferences on general shape differences between species. Only by including various factors in the model, and their interaction, can one arrive at the correct inference.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Now back  to your system. From what you have described you have a significant interaction, which, as you stated, implies that some aspect of sexual dimorphism differs between groups. That result demands further exploration and examination. How does sexual dimorphism differ? Is one species sexually dimorphic and the other not? Is the degree of sexual dimorphism greater in one population versus the other? Is the direction of sexual dimorphism similar of different in shape space? These are the questions to investigate now.  Note that trajectory analysis would be a particularly useful set of tools to utilize here; and in fact, have been used to examine and compare patterns of sexual dimorphism across groups (see Collyer and Adams, 2007; 2013: Adams and Collyer, 2007; 2009, etc.).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > To answer your last question about obtaining residuals separately for each population and using these; no.  That would be tantamount to the residuals from regression example above. Since the pop:sex interaction term is significant, residuals from a sex-model within populations are simply not comparable across them. Subsequent analyses into the nature of the sexual dimorphism are likely to be more fruitful in terms of extracting useful biological information.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Hope this helps,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Dean

> > > > > > > From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <http://googlegroups.com/> <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <http://googlegroups.com/>> On Behalf Of Nicole Torres Tamayo
> > > > > > > Sent: Tuesday, July 3, 2018 8:46 AM

> > > > > > > Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Dear Dr. Mike Collyer, all
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I performed a Procrustes ANOVA with procD.lm(shape ~ sex * population)
> > > > > > > and actually I found that there is a significant interaction between
> > > > > > > population and sex, in other words, my two populations differ in
> > > > > > > patterns of sexual dimorphism. Because of this, I can't correct my
> > > > > > > shape data for the effect of sex, because I would be
> > > > > > > sustracting a male/female mean shape to populations that do not have a
> > > > > > > common male/female mean shape.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > That said, does it mean that I would need to work with each population
> > > > > > > separately? I mean, should I remove the effect of sex from each
> > > > > > > population separately and analyze the residuals of each regression
> > > > > > > independently?
> > > > > > > Thank you very much in advance.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > All the best,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Nicole
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > 2018-06-26 15:11 GMT+02:00 Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>>:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Nicole,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I believe the advice you were given is that you should explicitly test whether there is a sex * population interaction.  If there is, you should not try to “correct” your shape data, as sexual dimorphism manifests differently in the different populations.  You can do that with
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > procD.lm(shape ~ sex * population)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If the  sex * population effect in the ANOVA is significant, do not correct shapes.  If not, you can use the residuals from a new model
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > which if added to the overall mean shape, will produce shapes that have held constant the effects of population and sex.  This is how I accomplish this:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > newshape <- procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population, iter = 1)$residuals + procD.lm(shape ~ 1, iter = 1)$fitted
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Keep in mind that you would also have to use arrayspecs to convert newshape back into an array rather than a matrix.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Again, the correction should be done IF, AND ONLY IF, you have determined there is not a meaningful interaction between sex and population.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Cheers!
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Mike
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to place a four sets of equidistant semilandmarks between four landmarks on a series of outlines. I was hoping to import the outlines in Momocs, use coo_slice to separate each outline into the four separate curves, and then use digit.curves in Geomorph to place the semilandmarks. In order to use coo_slice I converted the outlines to Out objects:

Outcoo<-list.files("path", full.names = TRUE) %>% import_jpg() %>% Out()
coo_ldk<-def_ldk(Outcoo, 4) %>% coo_slide(, ldk = 1)
curves<-coo_slice(coo_ldk, ldk = c(1,2,3,4))

Now I have a list of four sets of Opn objects - so far so good, but now I need to convert these to p-k-n arrays that can be read by digit.curves. Could you please advise how I can do this?

Thank you,
Joe

Joe,

I don’t know what an Opn object is but I suspect that it is also a list. If you have lists within a list, the simplify2array function won’t work but it combined with a lapply function to grab the coords from the Opn objects might work, assuming there is something like Opn$coords. For example,

coords <- lapply(curves, function(x) x$coords)

coords <- simplify2array(coords)

This is just a guess, assuming an Opn object is complex.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Semi-landmarks along a curve
messages.subject_clean: Semi-landmarks along a curve
messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon!

I’m interested to know if there is a function in geomorph that automatically lays semi-landmarks between fixed landmarks on a curve/edge (in 3D) – I’m thinking something similar to the buildtemplate function, in which you lay some fixed landmarks and it fills in the space with a certain number of semi-landmarks, except for a specific section of a 3D model rather than the whole thing (think iliac crest on an ilium, for example).  With both the digit.curves and define.sliders functions, if I understand correctly, all the landmarks have to be laid manually and then the sliders selected from those landmarks, so I’m interested to know if there is a more automated solution available in which a smaller number of fixed landmarks can be laid and the spaces between the fixed landmarks filled in automatically with semi-landmarks.

Thank you!

Sincerely,

Marla

messages.subject: Error for GLS with an interaction term
messages.subject_clean: Error for GLS with an interaction term
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have recently updated the geomorph package in my PC and since then I am receiving an error when I ran a GLS with interaction term in both procD.pgls and lm.rrpp.

The formulas I am using are the following:

#ProcD.pgls
gdf<-geomorph.data.frame(shape=gpa$coords, logCS=log10(gpa$), fam=fam)
procD.pgls(shape~logCS*fam, Tree, data=gdf)

#lm.rrpp
vcvTree<-vcv.phylo(Tree)
data.t=rrpp.data.frame(shape=gpa$coords, logCS=log10(gpa$),fam=fam)
lm.rrpp(shape~logCS*fam, Cov=vcvTree, data=data.t)

fam is the families (n=20) as character (I tried as.factor too).

The error I receive is the following:
"Error in fit.o$X %*% fit.cov$coefficients : non-conformable arguments"

Under OLS both functions work fine.
I have the suspect that is the number of family to prevent the computation of the GLS. The GLS is computed fine for interaction terms with less categories (e.g. 6).

Any help will be very much appreciated.
Thank you in advance,

Giada

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Error for GLS with an interaction term
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Error for GLS with an interaction term
messages.body_plain:
Giada,

It looks like the geomorph data frame entry for logCS has a mistake (missing object), but I am sure that would also return an error so I think this is only a mistake in the email.

The error comes at the end of the analysis for finding fitted values.  I assume that during the attempt to fit the model, you received a warning like this:

Warning: Because variables in the linear model are redundant,
the linear model design has been truncated (via QR decomposition).
Original X columns: 20
Final X columns (rank): 10
Check coefficients or degrees of freedom in ANOVA to see changes.

except that yours would have different numbers.  This would suggest that for some families, you have single observations?  So, your suspicion is correct, but it is actually a bug in geomorph too that for GLS, the code forgets to use QR decomposition on the original design matrix when attempting to find GLS fitted values; i.e., in my example above, fit.o$X has 20 columns but fit.cov$coefficients has only 10 coefficients after QR decomposition.  This is not an issue with OLS models because this particular calculation is not made.

We will update this as soon as we can.  Unfortunately, your error catches me at a conference, so my ability to debug might be a bit compromised at the moment.  Please be patient!

Cheers!
Mike

Giada,

I think I fixed this error, which actually occurs in the RRPP package on which geomorph depends.  You can update RRPP via Github with

devtools::install_github(“mlcollyer/RRPP”)

Restarting R and geomorph might be needed.  I would like to request some feedback on whether this solved your problem.  Without real data, my solution is a little speculative (it involved removing missing coefficients, which R returns as NA, and hoping the columns of X and rows of B match).  I simulated some data and it seemed to work, but I am working in a hypothetical space.  Please let me know if actual results seem correct.

I will update RRPP on CRAN maybe in a few weeks, with this patch, but the update on Github is immediate.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: help interpreting pairwise results in RRPP
messages.subject_clean: help interpreting pairwise results in RRPP
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm looking for feedback on using the new pairwise function in RRPP in place of the now-deprecated advanced.procD.lm, to make sure I am using the right test types (Type I) and models.

I have 3D landmark data and skull lengths (measured as condylobasal length [CBL]) for 100 skulls from 7 species spanning their postnatal development. Following Mike Collyer's examples  <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/geomorph/vignettes/geomorph.assistance.html>(thanks Mike!), I see that species is a significant effect by:

> fit.size <- procD.lm(Pcoords ~ logCBL, data = gdf, print.progress = FALSE) # simple allometry model

> fit.species<- procD.lm(Pcoords ~ logCBL * Species, data = gdf, print.progress = FALSE) # unique species allometries

> anova(fit.size, fit.species, print.progress = FALSE)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization

Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals

Number of permutations: 1000

Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares

Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

                           ResDf Df     RSS     SS      MS     Rsq      F      Z     P Pr(>F)

Pcoords ~ logCBL (Null)       98  1 1.61649                0.40762

Pcoords ~ logCBL * Species    86 12 0.28708 1.3294 0.11078 0.89480 33.188 18.416 0.001

Total                         99    2.72882

and that species have unique allometries:
> fit.common <- procD.lm(Pcoords ~ logCBL + Species, data = gdf, print.progress = FALSE) # common allometry. test of diffs in y-intercept
> fit.unique <- procD.lm(Pcoords ~ logCBL * Species,data = gdf, print.progress = FALSE) # unique allometries, species have diff slopes
> anova(fit.common, fit.unique, print.progress = FALSE)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

                                  ResDf Df     RSS      SS      MS     Rsq      F      Z     P Pr(>F)
Pcoords ~ logCBL + Species (Null)    92  1 0.44662                 0.83633
Pcoords ~ logCBL * Species           86  6 0.28708 0.15954 0.02659 0.89480 7.9655 20.132 0.001
Total                                99    2.72882

Although when I plot the prediction lines for the preferred model (unique allometries), they look strangely parallel, even though in the pairwise set up below I get significant slope angle differences for all but 4 species pairs, ranging from 23-47% angular differences.
plotAllometry(fit.unique, size = gdf$logCBL, logsz = FALSE, method = "PredLine", pch = 21, bg = as.numeric(gdf$Species), col = "black", cex = 1.5)

here is the regression score plot for comparison:
plotAllometry(fit.unique, size = gdf$logCBL, logsz = FALSE, method = "RegScore", pch = 21, bg = as.numeric(gdf$Species), col = "black", cex = 1.5)

For pairwise comparisons, I use the unique allometries fit as the null model:
> reveal.model.designs(fit.unique)

                         Reduced                               Full
logCBL                         1                             logCBL
Species                   logCBL                   logCBL + Species
logCBL:Species  logCBL + Species  logCBL + Species + logCBL:Species <- Null/Full inherent in pairwise
> PW <- pairwise(fit.unique, groups = gdf$Species, covariate = gdf$logCBL, print.progress = FALSE)
> summary(PW, test.type = "dist", confidence = 0.95) #diffs in slope vector lengths (magnitude)
> summary(PW, test.type = "VC", angle.type = "deg") #diffs in slope vector orientation (direction)

For the former I am unsure what the vector length units are, for example would a pairwise "d" of 0.1 mean that species vectors differ by 10% of the size variable, here skull length (logCBL)? For the latter I understand it as the species pairs with the smallest vector correlation "r" will also have the largest angle difference, which is true for my results.

Graphically I am also wondering how to interpret the difference between a standard PCA plot using
> plotTangentSpace(Y.gpasym$coords, groups = Species, pch = 21, warpgrids = FALSE)
and one from
> plotAllometry(fit.unique, size = gdf$logCBL, logsz = FALSE, method = "size.shape",  pch = 21, bg = as.numeric(gdf$Species), col = "black", cex = 1.5)
where the size vector (here, logCBL) is appended to the matrix of shape coordinates.

In the PCA to the left, the first axis is strongly positively correlated with logCBL: Pearson’s correlation r=0.84, p<0.00001, while the 2nd is not: r=0.16, p=0.1, so it's hard to imagine what is pulling some species further apart in the size-shape PCA to the right. I'm just wondering if there is an advantage to show/describe one over the other, given my data set is highly size-dependent as it covers species entire postnatal ontogenies.

Finally, I was interested to do a two-block PLS on shape and size following Mike's vignette, but when I try I get an error, although the data for A1 (logCBL) and A2 (the shape coordinates) come from the same geomorph data frame I have been using for every other test, and they all seem fine.
> PLS <- two.b.pls(gdf$logCBL, gdf$Pcoords, print.progress = FALSE)
Error: Mismatched specimen names for A1 and A2.

I realise this is all a lot to ask, but I would really appreciate any advice to make sure I'm on the right track! I also hope any answers might help other people running similar tests.

Thank you!
Christy

School of BioSciences, University of Melbourne / Museums Victoria

T: +61 3 8341 7423 E: christy...@unimelb.edu.au; chip...@museum.vic.gov.au

messages.body_plain:
Christy,

Some point by point comments below.

Cheers!
Mike

>  species have unique allometries...

>
> Although when I plot the prediction lines for the preferred model (unique allometries), they look strangely parallel, even though in the pairwise set up below I get significant slope angle differences for all but 4 species pairs, ranging from 23-47% angular differences.

Looks can be deceiving.  If you compare the red and the blue, for example, at size 3.5, their fitted shapes are perceptibly different but at size 5, they are the same (they are converging).  Now compare light blue and dark blue.  They have similar shapes at sizes 2 and 3 and similar shapes at 3 and 5, respectively.  They are diverging in shape with increased size.  Also, keep in mind these are PC1 values of shape and the angles in pairwise tests are in all dimensions.

> For pairwise comparisons, I use the unique allometries fit as the null model:
> > reveal.model.designs(fit.unique)
>
>                          Reduced                               Full
> logCBL                         1                             logCBL
> Species                   logCBL                   logCBL + Species
> logCBL:Species  logCBL + Species  logCBL + Species + logCBL:Species <- Null/Full inherent in pairwise
> > PW <- pairwise(fit.unique, groups = gdf$Species, covariate = gdf$logCBL, print.progress = FALSE)
> > summary(PW, test.type = "dist", confidence = 0.95) #diffs in slope vector lengths (magnitude)
> > summary(PW, test.type = "VC", angle.type = "deg") #diffs in slope vector orientation (direction)
>
> For the former I am unsure what the vector length units are, for example would a pairwise "d" of 0.1 mean that species vectors differ by 10% of the size variable, here skull length (logCBL)? For the latter I understand it as the species pairs with the smallest vector correlation "r" will also have the largest angle difference, which is true for my results.

The distance, d, between vector lengths is the difference in the amount of shape change per unit of size.  A loose way to interpret this is if you look at the allometry plot, the light blue slope is rising faster than the others.  The height change of light blue from say 2 to 3 is about 0.2.  For the dark blue from 3 to 4 it is maybe 0.15.  Since these are linear, the d between the two of them should be around 0.05; i.e., | 0.20 - 0.15 |.  Why do this?  Two vectors can be correlated in direction - the way shape changes with size - but one group can exhibit more shape change per unit size than the other.
>
> Graphically I am also wondering how to interpret the difference between a standard PCA… In the PCA to the left, the first axis is strongly positively correlated with logCBL: Pearson’s correlation r=0.84, p<0.00001, while the 2nd is not: r=0.16, p=0.1, so it's hard to imagine what is pulling some species further apart in the size-shape PCA to the right. I'm just wondering if there is an advantage to show/describe one over the other, given my data set is highly size-dependent as it covers species entire postnatal ontogenies.

In my opinion, no, there is no advantage for size-shape PCA.  I do not like shape-size PCA and I would never advocate using it.  We included it as a tool in the toolbox because presumably someone might have a purpose for it, but like those little hammers that can only hammer tacks, I find its appeal quite limited.

What the standard PCA and your correlation test reveal is that if one orientates the shape space with the axis that has the most information, that information appears to be allometry.  This is helpful to know.  The other PCA seems to augment shape differences, except they are not shape differences.  They are a conglomerate of shape and size, and the variables have different units and scales.  Note that in the latter, you might want to use asp = 1 as an argument to preserve aspect ratio, then the first PC will definitely be correlated with size.

>
> Finally, I was interested to do a two-block PLS on shape and size following Mike's vignette, but when I try I get an error, although the data for A1 (logCBL) and A2 (the shape coordinates) come from the same geomorph data frame I have been using for every other test, and they all seem fine.
> > PLS <- two.b.pls(gdf$logCBL, gdf$Pcoords, print.progress = FALSE)
> Error: Mismatched specimen names for A1 and A2.

Check the names of your objects; e.g.,

names(gdf$logCBL)
dimnames(gdf$Pcoords)

somewhere along the way you might have lost the specimen names in one of them but you can recover them; e.g.,

dimnames(gdf$Pcoords)[[3]] <- names(gdf$coords)

or

names(gdf$coords) <- dimnames(gdf$Pcoords)[[3]]

Because two.b.pls can work with data sets in different orders, it is essential to match up specimen names.  It seems in your case not to be able to do that.

Christy,

Since the Predline option is simply PC1 of the predicted values from the regression (or MANCOVA if multi-group), the simplest thing to do is go back one step to the mancova step, and use the predicted values from that. For this one fits the linear model, and then uses shape.predictor. The help file (and/or vignette) has an example for groups, and if I remember correctly, groups while accounting for a covariate. Yours is a similar situation.

As to the trajectory analysis error, what that means is that your second factor in the model does not have representation for all levels of the first factor. As an example, say I had species and sex, but for some reason I was not able to collect females for one species. That would cause a problem due to the lack of representation of that sub-level.
